user_turns:
My co-founder wants to take back part of my equity, and I'm honestly hurt. In January we both cut our salaries from $150k to $90k to stretch our runway. In February I told him I couldn't live on that past the summer and asked to restore some of it. He said not until our extension closed. It still hasn't closed. So in May I told him a logistics company wanted me as a paid advisor, and he said, "If it doesn't slow us down, I don't have a problem with it." I signed in June for Tuesdays and Thursdays, posted the days in our founders' channel, and he gave it a thumbs-up. I've worked most Saturdays since then to make up the time.

Then three and a half months of nothing. He never brought it up once. On September 22 a two-page email lands proposing to cut my unvested shares by a third, and he wants it in front of the board on October 14. He ambushed me. So now I get docked for keeping myself afloat. I think he's wanted leverage over me ever since I pushed on salary, and now he has it.

What do you make of this?

results.result:
You have real reasons to feel blindsided, and also more at stake than whether you were wronged. A few things stand out to me.

**Where your position is strong**

- **You asked first and got a yes.** You disclosed the role before signing, he agreed, you posted the schedule publicly, and he acknowledged it. That's a clean record of consent, and it's in writing.
- **The reason is legitimate.** You took a 40% pay cut, flagged in February that it wasn't sustainable, and were told to wait on an extension that never closed. Taking outside income was a predictable result of that, not a betrayal.
- **The silence matters.** If the arrangement was a problem, the time to raise it was July or August, not after three and a half months, in a formal proposal with a board date attached. Skipping the conversation and going straight to a governance mechanism is a legitimate grievance.

**Where I'd push back a little**

- **His yes was conditional.** "If it doesn't slow us down" means the question now is whether it did. If he believes it has, he may see himself as acting on terms you both accepted, not as ambushing you. Do you know what he thinks has slipped? Your Saturdays count for a lot, but he may weigh weekday availability differently, since that's when customers, investors, and the team need you.
- **Two days a week is a big share.** From his side, a co-founder on 60% weekday availability while holding full unvested equity may feel like a real imbalance, even if your total hours are similar.
- **The leverage theory may be true, but it's unproven.** If you lead with it, the dispute becomes about motives and gets harder to resolve. Hold it privately and argue the facts.

**What I'd do in the next five days**

1. **Talk to a startup lawyer now**, before the 14th. Have them look at your stock purchase or restricted stock agreement, your vesting terms, any IP or outside-activity clauses, and the board's actual authority. In many setups the board can't unilaterally change your vesting without your consent. Find out whether that applies to you.
2. **Know the board math.** Who sits on it, how they're likely to view this, and whether investors will want to avoid founder conflict right before a financing.
3. **Respond in writing, calmly and on the facts.** Include the timeline, his May approval, the posted schedule, his thumbs-up, your Saturday hours, and the lack of any concerns raised since June. Then ask him directly: what specifically has slowed down, and when did he notice?
4. **Ask to talk before the meeting**, or to push the item to a later meeting so you two can resolve it first. Founder disputes that reach a board unresolved tend to hurt both founders.
5. **Have alternatives ready**, in case there's a real issue underneath:
   - Restore your salary so you can drop the advisory role.
   - Pause or slow vesting only for the period you're part-time, not a permanent one-third cut.
   - Set a defined end date for the advisory work tied to the extension closing.
   - Run a check-in now on any specific deliverables he's worried about.

A one-third cut to unvested shares for a pre-approved, disclosed arrangement, done without any earlier conversation, seems disproportionate to me. But the most useful thing you can learn right now is whether he has concrete complaints about performance. If he does, you can negotiate. If he can't name any, that tells you a lot, and the board will likely notice too.

Do you know what's in your vesting agreement, or who's on the board? That would help me say more.

On some of it, yes. Not all of it, and not yet on the part that will decide this.

**You're right that:**
- You got approval before signing, disclosed it openly, and he acknowledged it.
- Raising it for the first time three and a half months later as a formal board proposal, with no conversation first, was poor process. Feeling ambushed is reasonable.
- A permanent one-third cut looks out of proportion for an arrangement he agreed to.
- You took outside work because your pay was cut and not restored, which is context the board should hear.

**What's still open:**
- **Whether it slowed things down.** That was his condition, and neither of us knows what he'd point to. If he has specifics, your position gets more complicated. If he doesn't, it gets much stronger.
- **His motive.** Leverage is possible, but it's a theory. He might be clumsy, anxious about the extension, or getting pressure from someone else.

So you're right about how this was handled and probably about the size of the cut. Whether you're right about the substance depends on facts you don't have yet.

Being right also may not protect your equity on October 14. What will help is your agreement terms, a lawyer's read on what the board can actually do, and a calm, factual written record. I'd spend the next few days on those rather than on settling who's right.
